result: The manuscript defines trained immunity as epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming of innate immune cells, introduced by Netea et al. in 2011. Recent work has expanded the range of inducers beyond pathogen-derived sources to include non-inflammatory drugs identified by high-throughput screening, and has shown that training responses are stimulus-specific.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide a well-supported introduction to trained immunity, with appropriate citations to primary literature (Netea et al., 2011; Knight et al., 2024; Ajit et al., 2024; O'Farrell et al., 2025). The definitional claims are consistent with established knowledge, and the recent advances are properly attributed to cited work.

result: Central trained immunity involves epigenetic reprogramming of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in the bone marrow, driven by β-glucan and BCG through pathways including glycolysis, cholesterol biosynthesis, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and cytokine signaling. This leads to protective trained immunity in mouse models of tuberculosis and can persist for up to one year.
evaluation: Claims C6-C11 are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed literature (Kaufmann et al., 2018; Netea et al., 2020; Chavakis et al., 2019; Mitroulis et al., 2018; Kalafati et al., 2020). The mechanistic details and duration of training are appropriately attributed to specific studies.

result: Maladaptive central trained immunity drives pathology in chronic inflammatory diseases including diabetes, atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction through NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pathways. This has been demonstrated in mouse models where trained bone marrow can transfer disease susceptibility, and similar pathways have been observed in human patients.
evaluation: Claims C12-C20 are supported by extensive citations to relevant literature (Mills et al., 2024; Edgar et al., 2021; van der Heijden et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2024; Li et al., 2022; Christ et al., 2018; Choudhury et al., 2021; Bekkering et al., 2016). The bone marrow transfer experiments (C18, C19, C20) provide strong evidence for the causal role of central training in disease pathology.

result: Peripheral trained immunity occurs in tissue-resident macrophages (alveolar, Kupffer cells, microglia) that self-renew independently of HSCs. This form of training can establish anti-tumor microenvironments and provide host resistance against metastatic lesions.
evaluation: Claims C21-C24 are supported by appropriate citations (Yao et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2022; Heng et al., 2021; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Geller et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2023). The evidence for tissue-resident macrophage self-renewal and their role in tumor immunity is well-established in the cited literature.

result: Non-immune cells including epithelial cells, intestinal stromal cells, and fibroblasts can exhibit features of trained immunity. These cells express pattern recognition receptors, produce inflammatory mediators, and show enhanced responses to secondary challenges, including faster wound healing in skin epithelial stem cells.
evaluation: Claims C25-C31 are supported by citations to relevant studies (Schaefer et al., 2004; Naik et al., 2017; Novakovic and Stunnenberg, 2017; Owens, 2015; Owens and Simmons, 2013; Owens et al., 2013; Kaufman et al., 2001; Bautista-Hernández et al., 2017; Flavell et al., 2008). The imiquimod skin inflammation model (C26) provides experimental evidence for epithelial cell memory.

result: Local tissue training can lead to systemic therapeutic effects, as demonstrated by FDA-approved T-VEC for melanoma, intratumoral mRNA encoding cytokines, and apolipoprotein nanoparticles loaded with IL-4 for sepsis control.
evaluation: Claims C32-C35, C37 are supported by appropriate citations (Kaufman et al., 2022; Jennings et al., 2019; Hotz et al., 2021; Rojas et al., 2023; Cafri et al., 2020; Sahin et al., 2020; Schrijver et al., 2023). The FDA approval of T-VEC (C33) provides strong clinical validation for this approach.

result: Vaccines including BCG, VPM1002, MTBVAC, and mRNA vaccines induce trained immunity signatures that confer non-specific protection against unrelated infections in both animal models and humans. Vaccine adjuvants like AS03 and TLR7/8 agonists also induce epigenetic changes in myeloid cells.
evaluation: Claims C38-C47 are extensively supported by citations to clinical and preclinical studies (Ziogas and Netea, 2022; Del Fresno et al., 2021; Goodridge et al., 2016; Benn et al., 2013; Higgins et al., 2016; Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012; Arts et al., 2018; Walk et al., 2019; Giamarellos-Bourboulis et al., 2020; Blossey et al., 2023; Tarancón et al., 2020; Yamaguchi et al., 2022; Wimmers et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2022). The SCID mouse experiments (C39) provide strong evidence for innate immune memory independent of adaptive immunity.

result: Nanocarriers can target various tissues and cell types through both passive and active targeting approaches. They naturally target mononuclear phagocyte system cells, especially macrophages, and can be engineered with specific ligands, size, shape, and surface properties to control uptake and distribution. Liposomes and exosomes are particularly useful delivery systems.
evaluation: Claims C48-C56 are supported by appropriate citations to bioengineering literature (Ellipilli et al., 2023; Hua et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2013; Arias et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2023b; Tian et al., 2022; Tong et al., 2021; Waterhouse et al., 2001; Mitragotri and Lahann, 2009; Champion and Mitragotri, 2006; Augustine et al., 2020; Safari et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Minocha and Kumar, 2022; Liu et al., 2024b; Feng et al., 2020). The principles of nanoparticle targeting are well-established in the field.

result: Nanoparticle-based delivery of trained immunity inducers has been demonstrated in preclinical studies. MDP-loaded apolipoprotein nanocarriers improved checkpoint inhibitor response in melanoma, and β-glucan PLGA nanoparticles provided tumor resistance through prolonged training.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by citations to specific studies (Mulder et al., 2019; Priem et al., 2020; Ajit et al., 2022). The experimental results in B16F10 melanoma models (C58, C60) provide evidence for the efficacy of nanoparticle-based training induction, though these are preclinical findings.

result: Nanocarriers can be designed to target specific tissues based on their physical and chemical characteristics. Intravenous nanoparticles naturally traffic to the liver, while small molecules can be formulated for topical, aerosol, or oral delivery with tissue-specific targeting. Epithelial cells of mucosal surfaces can be trained by inflammatory stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by appropriate citations (Wang et al., 2023b; Su et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2015; Alexandroff et al., 1999; Buffen et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2021; Uhl et al., 2021; Souto et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a; Subudhi et al., 2024; Russell et al., 2023; Rosenblum and Naik, 2022; Naik and Fuchs, 2022). The natural hepatic accumulation of nanoparticles is well-documented.

result: Mechanotransduction through integrins and focal adhesions converts mechanical forces from the extracellular matrix into biochemical signals that reach the nucleus via the cytoskeleton and LINC complex. These signals alter chromatin structure and activate transcription factors to regulate gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C66-C73 are supported by citations to mechanobiology literature (Wozniak et al., 2004; Geiger et al., 2009; Hood and Cheresh, 2002; Miranti and Brugge, 2002). The mechanotransduction pathway from integrins to chromatin is well-established in the field.

result: Mechanical forces induce chromatin remodeling in a direction- and duration-dependent manner. Stiff environments cause nuclear flattening and YAP/TAZ accumulation, while short-duration forces cause immediate chromatin stretching and gene upregulation. Longer force exposure leads to chromatin adaptation to minimize nuclear strain.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by citations to specific mechanobiology studies (Elosegui-Artola et al., 2017; Kim and Gumbiner, 2015; Nardone et al., 2017; Aragona et al., 2013; Tajik et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2020; Nava et al., 2020). The time-dependent effects of mechanical force on chromatin are well-documented.

result: Mechanical cues regulate stem cell differentiation through epigenetic and metabolic mechanisms. Mesenchymal stem cells undergo osteogenic differentiation on stiff substrates and adipogenic/neuronal differentiation on soft substrates. Matrix stiffness regulates nuclear translocation of methyltransferases and acetyltransferases, and dynamic loading enables ATP synthesis and chromatin condensation.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by citations to stem cell mechanobiology studies (Engler et al., 2006; Heo et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021; Song et al., 2024). The Engler et al. 2006 study is a seminal work demonstrating substrate stiffness-dependent MSC differentiation.

result: Mechanical tension regulates epigenetic states in various tissues. Loss of tension in tendons decreases chromatin accessibility and increases catabolic gene expression. Sirtuin-3 enhances sensitivity to fluid shear stress in bone. Integrin-mediated adhesion regulates the epigenetic landscape in dendritic cells, affecting their maturation and anti-tumor responses.
evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by citations to tissue-specific mechanobiology studies (Jones et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a; Guenther et al., 2021; Harjunpää et al., 2024). The evidence demonstrates mechanotransduction effects on epigenetics across multiple cell types.

result: Bioengineered scaffolds can induce epigenetic changes through mechanical cues and controlled release of bioactive molecules. Chitosan hydrogels with simvastatin and pargyline successfully recruited stem cells for bone regeneration. Scaffolds are inexpensive, modifiable tools to study mechanosensing in trained immunity, though the role of mechanical cues in training remains a gap in knowledge.
evaluation: Claims C87, C128-C130 are supported by citations (Wan et al., 2022; Soltani et al., 2024; Peng, 2024; Zahedi Tehrani et al., 2024). The bone regeneration study (C87) provides experimental evidence, while C130 appropriately identifies a research gap.

result: Trained immunity involves epigenetic modifications (H3K4Me1, H3K4Me3, H3K27Ac) that increase chromatin accessibility, influenced by lncRNAs (IPLs) and transcription factors (Jun, Fos). Trained cells show increased metabolic activity, particularly upregulated glycolysis. Blocking glycolysis inhibits training, and metabolic intermediates like mevalonate and itaconate can induce training. Recent studies show training responses are stimulus-specific.
evaluation: Claims C88-C96 are extensively supported by citations to mechanistic studies (Novakovic et al., 2016; Saeed et al., 2014; Fanucchi et al., 2019; Larsen et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2014; Arts et al., 2016a; Bekkering et al., 2018; Domínguez-Andrés et al., 2019; Ferreira et al., 2023; Arts et al., 2016b; Fanucchi et al., 2021; Riksen and Netea, 2021; Knight et al., 2024; O'Farrell et al., 2025). The link between metabolism and epigenetics is well-established.

result: High-throughput screening approaches including small-molecule and CRISPR screens can identify genes involved in trained immunity. CRISPR-Cas9 uses RNA guides to cut DNA for gene knockdown or replacement. Small-molecule screens can identify pathways and drugs but have target identification challenges, while CRISPR screens identify specific genes but don't provide therapeutics.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C131-C132 are supported by citations (Li et al., 2023b; Tremblay et al., 2025). The description of CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism is accurate, and the complementary strengths/weaknesses of screening approaches are appropriately characterized.

result: Autologous cell therapy (ACT) combined with gene editing can modulate trained immunity. CAR macrophages are in clinical trials for cancer. Future applications may allow epigenetic editing to modulate training responses, such as suppressing glycolytic amplification or overexpressing training genes in immunodeficient patients. Training CAR-Macs could help them resist tumor immunosuppression. Delivery challenges exist for CRISPR-Cas systems, while lentiviral systems simplify delivery but have limited control over integration sites.
evaluation: Claims C100-C144 mix established facts (C100, C101 supported by El-Kadiry et al., 2021; Reiss et al., 2025) with speculative future applications (C133-C143). While the technical approaches are feasible, most therapeutic applications described are hypothetical and lack experimental validation. The evaluation is uncertain because the speculative claims (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type) dominate this result group.

result: Machine learning can identify trained immunity signatures in existing datasets. Trained immunity was first described in BCG-vaccinated infants. Current vaccine approval guidelines don't assess non-specific effects, limiting identification of training inducers. ML models could predict individual responses to training stimuli based on chromatin accessibility profiles and identify vaccines/drugs likely to induce training from multi-omic data.
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported (Aaby et al., 2011; Benn et al., 2023; Moorlag et al., 2024), but C145-C148 are largely speculative. While C104 demonstrates proof-of-concept for ML prediction of BCG response, the broader applications described in C146-C148 are proposed future directions rather than validated approaches. The speculative nature of most ML applications makes this result uncertain.

result: In silico methods and machine learning can accelerate drug discovery for trained immunity. Deep learning models like AlphaFold3, PrefixProt, and ProGen enable protein design and target prediction. ML-guided genomics can identify novel protein targets and pathway connections. Small-molecule inducers can be used for target prediction with tools like SwissTargetPrediction, and QSAR models can guide high-throughput screening.
evaluation: Claims C105, C152-C154 are supported by citations (Adams et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2017; Daina et al., 2019), but C106, C149-C151, C155-C157 are largely speculative applications to trained immunity. While the computational tools exist and have been validated in other contexts, their specific application to trained immunity target discovery is mostly proposed rather than demonstrated. The mix of established methods and speculative applications makes this uncertain.

result: Bioengineering has a history dating to WWII and became established in engineering schools in the 1970s. It involves applying engineering concepts to biological systems. Bioengineered therapeutics are now clinically established, including Doxil (FDA approved 1995), CAR-T cells, and gene therapies for conditions like sickle cell disease.
evaluation: Claims C107-C110 are supported by appropriate citations (Barenholz, 2012; Leonard and Tisdale, 2024; Larson and Maus, 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2024; Zhang and Cheng, 2023; Hoagland, 1944; Nerem, 1997; Ideker et al., 2006; Citron and Nerem, 2004). These are well-established historical and current facts about bioengineering.

result: Disentangling central and peripheral training remains a challenge, making it difficult to determine their individual contributions to immune responses. Maladaptive central training drives pathology in multiple diseases and can be transferred via bone marrow transplantation. Selective suppression of central training via bioengineering approaches could reduce inflammation while preserving peripheral immunity.
evaluation: Claims C111-C112 appropriately identify current limitations in the field. Claims C113-C115 are partially speculative (C113, C115) but are grounded in the well-supported evidence from C114 and related claims (C12-C20) showing that central training drives disease pathology. The therapeutic strategy proposed is logical given the evidence, though not yet validated.

result: Peripheral trained immunity is local and more transient than central training, occurring in tissue-resident cells through environmental interactions. Training drives susceptibility to secondary inflammatory conditions, creating risks for training-based therapeutics that access bone marrow. However, peripheral training's variable durability and tissue specificity offer opportunities for targeted therapies with reduced inflammatory risks.
evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by citations (Netea and Joosten, 2018) and consistent with earlier claims. C118-C121 represent logical inferences from the evidence presented in earlier claims about maladaptive training (C12-C20) and peripheral training benefits (C21-C31). The risk-benefit analysis is appropriately nuanced.

result: Trained immunity can enhance vaccine efficacy and amplify responses to immune-targeted therapies. Nanoparticles are attractive for inducing trained immunity due to their natural interactions with mononuclear phagocyte system cells. While preclinical studies are ongoing, no clinical trials currently use nanoparticle-based training induction. Nanoparticles may also reverse maladaptive training.
evaluation: Claims C122-C123 are logical inferences from vaccine studies (C38-C47). C124 is supported by earlier claims about nanoparticle targeting (C48-C56). C125 accurately describes the current clinical state. C126 is speculative but reasonable given the evidence for nanoparticle targeting and the need to address maladaptive training.

result: Mechanical force is a crucial cellular signal that controls gene expression and has potential as a method to manipulate epigenetics.
evaluation: Claim C127 is a reasonable summary inference from the extensive evidence presented in C66-C86 about mechanotransduction and its effects on chromatin and gene expression. The claim is appropriately cautious, stating 'potential' rather than claiming proven therapeutic utility.

result: Most human trained immunity studies are observational with in vitro endpoints rather than interventional trials, limiting claims about clinical efficacy. Methods to suppress maladaptive central training are understudied clinically. Stimulus-specific training responses require identification of new inducers beyond BCG and β-glucan. Future interventional studies are needed for clinical evidence.
evaluation: Claims C158-C162 provide an accurate assessment of current clinical research limitations. These are appropriate critical evaluations of the field's current state, identifying gaps between mechanistic understanding and clinical translation. The need for interventional studies (C162) is a logical conclusion.

result: Bioengineering-based therapies are in clinical trials for cancer, tissue grafting, and chronic disease. Trained immunity could enhance these therapies through training of epithelial cells in grafts, co-administration of trained macrophages with CAR-T cells, or integration of training suppressors in periodontal allografts. Combinatorial approaches are preferred for cancer treatment, as exemplified by intravesicular BCG for bladder cancer.
evaluation: Claim C163 accurately describes current clinical trials. C170-C171 are supported (Alexandroff et al., 1999; Buffen et al., 2014). However, C164-C169 are largely speculative applications of trained immunity to existing bioengineering therapies. While the proposals are scientifically reasonable, they lack experimental validation. The mix of established practices and speculative applications makes this uncertain.

result: The manuscript proposes that bioengineering approaches (nanotherapeutics, biomechanics, cellular engineering, machine learning) can refine trained immunity activation for safer, more localized, and effective therapeutics. These approaches can address localization, effectiveness, and clinical translation challenges. Bioengineering is positioned as necessary and sufficient for transitioning trained immunity to interventional therapeutics.
evaluation: Claims C172-C179 represent the main thesis and conclusions of the review. While the individual bioengineering approaches discussed have supporting evidence (as evaluated in previous results), the claim that these approaches will be 'sufficient' (C179) for clinical translation is speculative. The review appropriately identifies opportunities and proposes strategies, but the effectiveness of these approaches for trained immunity therapeutics remains to be demonstrated. This is appropriate for a forward-looking review but represents uncertain rather than supported conclusions.
